The pan flute is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.112. Its construction rests on the stopped-pipe principle: it consists of several tubes of gradually increasing length, closed at one end, and the player blows across the top, so that the airstream passes over the inner edge of the opening and makes the sound. Each tube is tuned to one fundamental, and overblowing produces overtones. It is common in folk music and is used in Europe, Asia, the Americas and Africa; the traditional ensembles of Peru, Andean music, the cylindrical instruments of Laos and Thailand, and traditional African ensembles all have their variants.

The pan flute is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.112. The tubes are mostly made of bamboo, giant reed or a local cane, though wood, plastic, metal and clay also appear. The tuning parts vary with tradition: in the South American type small pebbles or dried corn kernels are dropped into the bottom of the tube; the Romanian curved type commonly uses beeswax, and also cork or rubber stoppers. The small chiflo is traditionally drilled from a block of wood, and modern ones are also cast in plastic. The other parts are not stated.
pan flute 以橫向氣流吹過管口內緣發聲。初學先持穩琴管，使一端封閉的管口: The pan flute sounds when a lateral airstream passes over the inner edge of the pipe opening. Begin by holding the pipes steady with the closed ends upward, aiming the airstream at the sharp inner edge to sound the fundamental of a single pipe; then practise overblowing with more pressure and tighter lips to reach an overtone close to a twelfth. On the Romanian curved type the player can turn the head or move the instrument with the hand to reach the notes, and for semitones tilts the opening and narrows the aperture with the jaw. Vibrato can be controlled with the hand or the airstream. For tuning, use wax, cork or rubber stoppers, or the traditional South American pebbles and dried corn kernels at the bottom of the pipes.
排笛作為氣鳴樂器，可於安地斯音樂與秘魯傳統團體、玻利維亞 jula-jula 與: As an aerophone, the pan flute can be heard in Andean music and the traditional ensembles of Peru, in the Bolivian jula-jula and julu-julu, and in recordings of the Romanian curved pan flute. The Thai wot is used in Isan folk music; the African ngororombe is often played with percussion in northeastern Zimbabwe, and the Nyungwe of Malawi also use it to accompany a dance of the same name. The Italian firlinfeu, and the chiflo / xipro of Portugal, Spain, Argentina and Mexico, are instruments of folk occasions; the African-American quills can be heard on recordings by Henry Thomas and are also associated with the Delta blues musician Sid Hemphill.
排笛屬氣鳴樂器，以端吹方式使氣流掠過管口內緣，在封閉管中形成駐波；管長決定基頻，: The pan flute is an aerophone: the player blows across the opening so that the airstream passes the inner edge and forms a standing wave in the stopped pipe; the length of the pipe sets the fundamental, and each pipe holds one fixed fundamental. The bore affects the timbre, narrow pipes tending towards a reedy sound and wide ones towards a fluty one. Overblowing a cylindrical pipe produces odd-numbered overtones close to a twelfth, while a tapering bore can approach an octave jump. The range depends on the number of pipes and on their lengths; on the Romanian curved pan flute the player can turn the head or move the instrument to reach the notes, and tilts the opening and uses the jaw to play sharps and flats. Volume control is not clearly documented, but overblowing needs more air pressure and tighter lips, and breath vibrato makes the level rise and fall with the diaphragm or the throat muscles. Unlike a single end-blown pipe, the pan flute sounds from several pipes.
排笛屬氣鳴樂器，古希臘稱Syrinx，與牧神Pan及森林仙女Syrinx傳說相關: The pan flute is an aerophone. In ancient Greece it was called the syrinx, and it is bound up with the myth of the god Pan and the forest nymph Syrinx; the Etruscans later used it at festivals and banquets, and the Romans used it at banquets, festivals, religious rites and funeral processions. Traditional Andean pan flutes are usually lashed together in rows, and they are common in the traditional ensembles of Peru and in Andean music; on the Bolivian highlands they are called jula-jula and in the mountains julu-julu. In the 1970s Romanian musicians made the curved pan flute known and spread it through Europe, Asia and the Americas; Laos and Thailand have the wot, and Africa has traditional forms such as the ngororombe.
